analysis.one_liner: Uses federal buying power to get childhood vaccines to states free and create registries to track kids' shots.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 22 House members from both parties, never got a committee vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given states federal grants to buy childhood vaccines at the low bulk price the government negotiates and hand them to doctors free, so no child would miss a shot because of cost. It also would have required vaccine makers to sell to states at the same low price they give the federal government, and funded state registries that remind parents when a child is due for a vaccine. The bill died in a House committee without ever coming up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Families of young children, especially the roughly one in four children under six on Medicaid and uninsured children whose parents pay out of pocket for shots, would get vaccines at no charge. State budgets would save money by buying in bulk instead of reimbursing doctors at retail prices. Parents would get automatic reminders when their child is due for a vaccination.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with young children and state health programs

how_it_helps.text: States would buy childhood vaccines at the federally negotiated bulk rate and distribute them to any provider free of charge, and providers could charge families only an administration fee, not the cost of the vaccine, and could not turn away a child whose family could not pay the fee.

The bill cites federal findings that fewer than half of preschool children were fully immunized, that more than 55,000 people caught measles in a three-year epidemic and 89 died in 1990 alone, and that a $25 measles shot can prevent a $7,000 hospitalization.
States could save money by purchasing in bulk rather than reimbursing providers the retail cost of vaccines given to children covered by Medicaid.
State health agencies would run immunization registries that record each child's shots and notify parents when the next vaccine is due, with grants of $5 million to $10 million a year.

analysis.who_pays: Vaccine manufacturers would bear the cost: they could be barred from selling any childhood vaccine to the federal government unless they agreed to sell it to states at the same low federal price. Taxpayers would fund the grants, authorized at $20 million to $30 million a year for the purchase program.

drawbacks.text: The registries would require every licensed health care provider, as a condition of their state license, to report each child's name, address, vaccine, and provider to a central state data system, raising the familiar privacy concerns that come with government health databases even though sharing a child's record with another provider would require a parent's consent.

Requiring manufacturers to match their lowest federal price for sales to states is a price control; an honest supporter would acknowledge it could squeeze maker margins on childhood vaccines, and critics of such clauses argue that squeezing margins risks supply or investment in new vaccines.

The grant program was modest relative to the problem the bill itself describes: $20 million to $30 million a year to reach the roughly half of preschoolers not fully immunized, with grants renewable for only two additional years before the program would need reauthorization.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit-cost case for families is strong on the bill's own terms: a $25 measles shot prevents a $7,000 hospitalization, and bulk buying is cheaper than paying retail. The real limitations are scale — the authorized funding is small against a problem the bill says touches more than half of preschoolers — and the trade-off that squeezing vaccine prices and building mandatory reporting registries carry genuine costs in supplier incentives and data privacy.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then passed to its Health and the Environment subcommittee two weeks later, and never came up for any vote before the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Louise Slaughter introduced the bill on August 5, 1992, and 22 colleagues — 18 Democrats and 4 Republicans — signed on as cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never reported the bill.
On September 14, 1992, the bill was referred to the subcommittee on Health and the Environment, where it sat with no further action through the end of the Congress on January 3, 1993.
No committee, subcommittee, or floor vote on the bill appears anywhere in its action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Vaccine manufacturers kept selling childhood vaccines at retail prices rather than matching the federal bulk rate, and no federal money flowed to states for free vaccines or registries under this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Vaccine manufacturers and status quo pricing

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship leaned Democratic — 18 of 22 cosponsors — but 4 Republicans signed on, and no vote was ever taken that would show how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill would bar federal procurement of any childhood vaccine unless the maker agreed to sell it to states at the same low federal bulk price, and free government distribution to providers would displace retail sales. The makers' interest in keeping retail pricing ran against families getting free shots.

Providers would receive vaccines free instead of buying them, but could charge only an administration fee, not the vaccine's cost, and could not refuse a child whose family could not pay that fee. Mostly aligned with the public benefit, with a real cost to their billing.

industries.industry: State and local public health agencies
industries.note: States would get $20 million to $30 million a year to buy vaccines cheaply and $5 million to $10 million a year for registries, cutting what they spend reimbursing providers at retail prices. Their interest runs directly alongside children's access to shots.
